    "thumbnail": "https://i.ytimg.com/vi/Hrbq66XqtCo/maxresdefault.jpg",
    "description": "I asked Jensen about TPU competition, Nvidia’s lock on the ever more bottlenecked supply chain needed to make advanced chips, whether we should be selling AI chips to China, why Nvidia doesn’t just become a hyperscaler, how it makes its investments, and much more. Enjoy!\n\n+𝐄𝐏𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐃𝐄 𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐊𝐒\n* Transcript: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/jensen-huang\n* Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/jensen-huang-tpu-competition-why-we-should-sell-chips/id1516093381?i=1000761582962\n* Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/episode/1viBRy6dQdlSw0OdFvogXB?si=bc2cdbd467ed4ee3\n\n𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐍𝐒𝐎𝐑𝐒\n- Crusoe's cloud runs on state-of-the-art Blackwell GPUs, with Vera Rubin deployment scheduled for later this year. But hardware is only part of the story—for inference, Crusoe's MemoryAlloy tech implements a cluster-wide KV cache, delivering up to 10x faster TTFT and 5x better throughput than vLLM. Learn more at https://crusoe.ai/dwarkesh\n\n- Cursor helped me build an AI co-researcher over the course of a weekend. Now I have an AI agent that I can collaborate with in Google Docs via inline comment threads! And while other agentic coding tools feel like a total black-box, Cursor let me stay on top of the full implementation. You can try my co-researcher out at https://github.com/dwarkeshsp/ai_coworker, or get started on your own Cursor project today at https://cursor.com/dwarkesh\n\n- Jane Street spent ~20,000 GPU hours training backdoors into 3 different language models, then challenged my audience to find the triggers. They received some clever solutions—like comparing the base and fine-tuned versions and extrapolating any differences to reveal the hidden backdoor—but no one was able to solve all 3. So if open problems like this excite you, Jane Street is hiring. Learn more at https://janestreet.com/dwarkesh\n\nTo sponsor a future episode, visit https://dwarkesh.com/advertise.\n\n𝐓𝐈𝐌𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐀𝐌𝐏𝐒\n00:00:00 – Is Nvidia’s biggest moat its grip on scarce supply chains?\n00:16:25 – Will TPUs break Nvidia’s hold on AI compute?\n00:41:06 – Why doesn’t Nvidia become a hyperscaler?\n00:57:36 – Should we be selling AI chips to China?\n01:35:06 – Why doesn’t Nvidia make multiple different chip architectures?",

      "text": "Dwarkesh's logic is: What NVIDIA holds in its hands is technology, and technology is something that shouldn't be easily given to competitors.\nJensen got anxious immediately after hearing this, and his wording became increasingly harsh, finally blurting out: \"That is a loser mindset, it makes no sense at all.\"\nDwarkesh is thinking about \"don't let competitors get the weapons.\"\nJensen is thinking \"what I'm building is an ecosystem, and the word 'competitor' doesn't even exist in an ecosystem.\"\nOne is calculating accounts, the other is laying out a grand strategy.       "text": "I respect Dwarkesh's willingness to ask ridiculous questions. It seemed to trigger Jensen because he probably has to deal with so many of the same misconceptions in Washington. But if Deepseek only optimizes for Huawei and they ship together, we risk losing half of the nuclear scientists (cuda devs + ai researchers) and potentially more if prestige drops and Chinese immigrants jump ship. Then losing half of the actual nukes (ai usage) because most of the world cannot afford American models, and also losing half our share of the world's enriched uranium (gpus).\n\nJensen describes GPUs advantage in being programmable and the ecosystem otherwise ASICs would be winning. So if Deepseek and other Chinese models leave Nvidia, then any Chinese model running on CUDA would have to develop optimizations which can take months. Huawei gains leverage in selling hardware to any country or open source user. Their hardware is a lot cheaper and most of the world would run on Huawei chips. While about half of the former CUDA devs leave the Nvidia ecosystem to work on Huawei which would be a disaster for the moat. If Nvidia tanks then American AI tanks which explains the circular investing (bubble?).       "text": "Basically this Indian doesn’t like Nvidia selling the chips to China, did you get it?",
      "like_count": 0,

      "author": "@alm-to2pz",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_ndpiHf65Z84lfZGmBP9Sw6o10Yr-iWzCHhNG8aag=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgwjHY3agDQtuG8qrjR4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I think Jensen's on the right side of history on this one. He's thinking in decades as against a more short-term view. The current dominance of the US in desktop (and all other) computing today rests on the duopoly of the IOS and Windows ecosystems. If a third, non-US force had been allowed to exist (because the Americans hoarded their tech), that force would have geopolitical will to compete and potentially wrest market share from the hegemony. It's noteworthy that while Android still controls 70% of the mobile market in China, HarmonyOS is the fastest growing. Anyone familiar with exponential progress knows that Android market share loss is now inevitable not just in China, but everywhere the Chinese mobile ecosystem controls (Africa, Southeast Asia, Latin America, and India). China and the global south represent about half of the world's population. \n\nImplementing the same protectionist strategy in AI will have far more dire consequences for the protectionists, not least because the industry is at its infancy. For the first time since the personal computer, the technology stack will not be the exclusive preserve of a single nation. What a time to be alive!",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCS0JCeq4FMVPVM6CRnNL51g",
      "author": "@tayofasunon1657",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_k7LQBI8f7fqkyOESrGXUKSoUiaOZHJx6vZAcZRPgmRXg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The China section was over the proposition -- Nvidia should sell their chips to China.\n\nJensen's argument was that American companies compete in the global economy as well as the American economy. If Nvidia only sells China the least advanced chips, China could still beat the American labs because China has the energy needed for a higher compute output. I do not think that Jensen had an answer to his rebuttal.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "Jensen’s logic feels inconsistent, to be honest. He runs a private company whose primary goal is profit..so of course he wants to sell more advanced chips to as many markets as possible?\n\nAt the same time, he openly acknowledges that China has massive advantages: huge energy capacity, deep funding, and a large pool of highly skilled computer scientists and engineers and even their own capabilities to make their own chips. Then he also says the U.S. has strong infrastructure, talent, and innovation-which is fair.\n\nBut after admitting strengths on both sides, he still seems overly confident that the U.S. will definitely stay ahead and that China won’t surpass it?That kind of certainty feels questionable-almost like claiming to predict the future with absolute confidence? \n\nGiven China’s scale, talent base, and the pace of progress over the last 30 years, it’s not unreasonable to think that the next 30 years could shift the balance significantly. Assuming one side will lead “for sure” ignores how dynamic and competitive this space really is.",
      "like_count": 1,

      "text": "Oh god, how is this interviewer just don’t understand the most basic thing that Jensen is saying? \n\nJensen is saying that China will get compute regardless if they buy from Nvidia or not because they will just make shit loads more 7nm chip (yes not as powerful but plenty of powerful enough), China can out manufacture US in that way because data center is an energy bottleneck issue not actual chip issue. Also Jensen have point out many times (and ignore by the interviewer) that you don’t need massive compute to create mythos and china already has the compute capacity to train model like mythos, paired together with 50% of the AI researcher are in China, china is going to be able to do it. So rather than thinking just by limiting China from American compute (Nvidia) will stop them, it is better to work with them so that no one will use the tech stack that way. I really don’t understand why is it so difficult for the interviewer to understand that. The interviewer seems to think that only Anthropic Claude can come up with a model like mythos. I am pretty sure there are plenty of model from China that can already does that that we don’t know about it. \n\nBefore this interview, I also thought banning chip sales to China is a good, but after this interview, I actually think Jensen Hwang actually has the best argument here.       "text": "🇨🇳 from China come to watch the debate：大胡子说城门楼子，黄仁勋说胯骨肘子，两个人的格局眼界根本完全不一样。一个是在行业内的顶级权威，一个是完全代表了典型的美国小市民的门外汉形象。我专门从中国来翻墙看你们吵架，笑死了。\n但是不得不承认黄仁勋真厉害，因为我们所有的中国人🇨🇳都知道，你英伟达不卖芯片给中国，中国迟早会在AI 赛道上发展出一个自给自足的生态。就像当年微软x86操作系统在中国无数盗版，而比尔盖茨故意无视一样，导致中国到现在也发展不出自己的国产操作系统。\n其实到底卖不卖芯片给中国，最关键的逻辑是你如果要遏制中国，你最好是直接把他的AI一把掐死，0发展。不然得益于中国的独特国情，包括庞大的内需市场科研人才无限能源等，这股庞大的国家市场的力量会推动着中国的AI一直朝前发展，到时候美国不仅芯片卖不出去，大模型的智能化也被追赶上就会吃大亏。所以黄仁勋的意思就是我们必须有平衡的和中国合作，因为美国也能从中国的发展之中也获取巨大的利益。包括他的公司。\n总而言之，大家站的角度不一样，谁也说服不了谁。🤣笑死了",

      "id": "Ugx4iq5lOVxa89Zi9494AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "My view is that Nvidia is generating enormous revenue because it is producing AI chips at very large scale. The issue, as I see it, is that the United States may not have enough electrical capacity to fully support all of the AI hardware Nvidia can produce. If demand in the U.S. becomes constrained by power availability, Nvidia could eventually face pressure to slow production unless it finds other buyers that not only want the chips, but can also afford them and supply the electricity needed to run them. China could be one of the few countries large enough to absorb a substantial share of that excess capacity.\n\nLooking further ahead, there is also the question of what happens to AI chips already installed in U.S. data centers when newer and more advanced chips come to market. If older chips are replaced, a secondary market would need to exist for that used hardware. One possible solution would be to sell those older chips to other countries that still have demand for them, and China might be a major potential buyer.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The reason Jensen gets so worked up is because Dwarkesh doesn’t understand or acknowledge what Jensen is really trying to say nor does he really try to understand. Dwarkesh is constantly trying to frame and make a point rather than expand and ask Jensen about the point he’s trying to make. Jensen has to explicitly deny Dwarkesh’s off topic claims multiple times, and that’s not something the guest should have to do. \nJensen is making the claim that people who claim that preventing NVIDIA chips from the Chinese market to hurt the Chinese AI tech are doing the opposite because it promotes Chinese advancement of their own chips and ecosystem for AI growth. And he claims this by stating that China has the best and numerous AI engineers as well as the most abundant energy ready to be used for AI. Jensen is claiming that by making the Chinese AI ecosystem continue to use NVIDIA chips, China is unable or slower in advancing their own homegrown chips, which benefits the US. Dwarkesh is making analogies that are honestly an insult to Jensen and his company. It really is absurd for him to say those things while Jensen is trying to make these points. It would have been a lot better if he were to first try to understand what Jensen is saying by trying to clarify instead of constantly trying to go towards the counter arguments without acknowledging Jensen’s viewpoints. I think Jensen handled the interview well. I feel sorry for him that the viewers don’t seem to understand what he was even saying.",

      "id": "UgxSqldlKGB8WbOQMcR4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Yall acting like Dwarkesh Destroyed Jensen, but I think his point at 1:20 is a strong compelling argument, but also big ups to this interviewer pushing Jensen hard enough that such a strong multifaceted discussion can come out for us to analyse. Both sides have valid points. \n\nJensen Believes Getting Money, Market share and usage from China keeps USA Ahead by getting more in USA's Tech Stack and moat, as China will be strong regardless thanks to the advantage of their developers, and taking away reasons for using USA Hardware prevents this reliance and drain of resources to the USA, which couldve helped the USA Tech stack strengthen. \n\nDwarkesh is arguing that since there is precedent for China and other tech companies ability to switch to other processors, and that China is Stronger with AI, not giving them NVIDIA helps preserve Americas lead.\n\nJensen disagrees that switching processors is Easy, and also feels that Preserving lead in tech is possible, since the leverage of computer science far outweighs the leverage of Compute's Scale, and China wins on that, which is valid. \n\nHe believes having the High Leverage of Development built on USA's Stack, enhancing and Enriching as well as building reliance on it is what keeps USA Ahead. I think this is a valid argument. While switching Systems is possible, the major dominant player once things reach a level of a new status quo will probably still have the most reliance from others, and its likely their moat will keep growing, as much as people are trying to erode it.\n\nTLDR: Jensen Believes Selling Chips Builds Reliance on USA, which allows the resources to be funneled into more advances that builds more reliance, and moves the highest leverage actors in the stack, the Devs, onto USA's Hardware, as he believes the reliance, the moat will continue and grow, and make it harder to swap to other processors. As expected, Jensen is bullish on NVIDIA's Moat and prospects.\n\nDwarkesh believes no chip = slower ai, and that China Can switch even if they were reliant on NVIDIA to get there in the first place. \n\nFascinating argument that I cant draw the answer as I am no expert, but plenty of unique and enriching perspectives and theories that help expand my mind shared here",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Spicy Jensen is revealing: it's clear what he wants (unfettered access to a largely untapped market) and that safety a very distant secondary/tertiary/etc. concern. Even if he is right, that the sum of all fears could be accomplished today, already, by any motivated 'bad actor', it would still be nice to hear some at-least lip service that a) China's mode of production, and its attendant cultural/societal implications, is inherently adversarial to that of the United States' and b) that 'accelerated computing' has advanced to the point where it has real-world geopolitical implications. He doesn't really acknowledge any of this (other than repeating that the U.S. should be/remain 'ahead') which should be troubling both to audience segments steeped in this debate as well as those coming to it fresh. The question that (perhaps) went unasked is: why aren't you worried about liability? Maybe he feels that hardware is abstracted enough from any specific use case that it's free of accountability for any widespread negative consequences (which would put him in good company with corps. like Raytheon and Boeing). I suppose we'll see if his tune changes once recursive self-improvement becomes widespread among not only frontier but also open-weight models.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The bigger picture -a enriched Uranium correlation doesn't work. The argument is looking at past tense what ifs for justifications. Fact - It is in the past. China's Nvidia chips aren't the cutting edge but are sought after due to how well they integrate. Demand is high for all levels of their chips at an almost fundamental level. Opening up your largest semiconductor company to the world and getting their sticky software gives you a technological and economic muscle to leverage. You saw Trump do this already. These sales backfeed into the system(nvda investment) further feeding development and maintaining the ability for cutting edge development while also leaving from, for sake of comparison, smaller bread crumbs for everyone else - Making it a win/win condition and increasing the demand and need for US Tech Stacks in the world. If you want to play the enriched uranium as an argument lets talk about the USD and Oil and maybe it'll start to make sense. Speaking in absolutes about past what if situations is weak stance and discorrelated. However, it was awesome to watch this debate. If you isolate yourself, the world keeps developing around you (North Korea) and then they don't need you anymore. You lose access to the club because they have self developed better tech and the advantage US Tech Stacks lose adoption.\n\nShould we stop selling F-150s to rest of the world because they put 50cals on the back of some of them?",

      "id": "UgzopyBoIoTCdL8bQiR4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "comparing ai / chips to enriched uranium (1:17:50) is crazy. that argument goes down a slippery slope that even us citizens should not have wide access to it. for ai to be helpful and pose a net positive to humanity, it must stay open and accessible to everyone at reasonable cost and leverage.\n\ni came in skeptical since jensen has financial incentive for NVDA to sell more, but the interviewer's strange line of questioning and rude badgering made me side more with jensen. additionally, if america decides as a nation to limit NVDA because they are \"critical to national security\", might china not be more incentivized to create their own chips which may even be better? this has been done before in other industries. surely the short time bought by this action would not be worth it to america as a whole. it might be \"illegal\" to sell chips directly to china, but they are still smuggled there regardless through third parties etc. despite this, america is still winning.\n\nopening the trade curtain enables nvidia to continue to lead the ai revolution without encouraging possibly backdoored or hardware limited chinese chip companies to be fostered. \n\nthe fact is that anyone could have made mythos. anthropic just publicly got there first. if china were first and chose to close source it and block america from using it due to \"safety concerns\" military action certainly would be threatened. but when anthropic does this systematically to all of china for ALL models, it is fine. as an american, it is clear that there is a factor of hypocrisy at play here. \nchina are the ones systematically open weighing their models. usa hasn't been (other than gemma 4). if these open weight models are built on nvidia infrastructure rather than some proprietary chinese-only chips and architecture, americans can no longer benefit from their research. it is therefore in the interest of the us to allow the chip trade on the condition that chinese frontier labs continue to openweight their models and provide rare earth minerals. \n\nnvidias value is in its architecture and ecosystem. you NEED chinese developers to build on CUDA etc rather than their own systems. as much as i came in with skeptical ears knowing that jensen has financial incentives, jensen's absolutely right here. \n\nthe conversation is helpful and important, but the slogan of \"well researched interviews\" does not hold in that specific instance. i felt that segment was too elementary and naive from the interviewer's part.",

      "text": "Jensen s an impressive human.  But remember kids. Ultimate power corrupts ultimately.  I believe this is true almost always.  I think he's acting in the best interests of his company.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "Dwarkesh's red-team argument has some gaping holes\n\ndwarkesh's red team argument is that if you turn any of these levers to 0 the entire output can be made 0 - (only paper does it work like that)\n\nadvanced_capabilities = \na_chips * \nb_flops * \nc_flops_per_watt * \nd_total_watts_of_energy * \ne_researchers * \nf_datacenters * \ng_model_architecture * \nh_algorthmic_increase_in_throughput * \ni_friendly_policies * \n(j_black_swan_innovations)\n\n\n\njensen's blue team argument is more realistic and 100% corrrect - no one controls the entire lever by themselves - so the equation is more like \n\nadvanced_capabilities = \nmax(1, a_chips) * \nmax(1, b_flops) * \nmax(1, c_flops_per_watt) * \nmax(1, d_total_watts_of_energy) * \nmax(1, e_researchers) * \nmax(1, f_datacenters) * \nmax(1, g_model_architecture) * \nmax(1, h_algorthmic_increase_in_throughput) * \nmax(1, i_friendly_policies) * \nmax(1, j_black_swan_innovations)\n\nwhere each variable is a vector of options. if any vector's max is less than the unit factor then it makes no sense to use that \n(if driving to work took longer + costed more + required more effort - why wouldn't you just walk lol)",

    {
      "id": "UgwV1usyctTVB5XHzuR4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Jensen is right. The saying, “Keep your allies close and your enemies closer,” has never been more relevant. The way the U.S. is blocking China’s access to NVIDIA chips, then bailing out Intel and asking Elon to strike deals with Intel, is fundamentally anti-capitalist. Like Jensen said, if you lose, you lose. We should not be intervening like this.\n\nMore importantly, having China rely on our technology may be the smartest move, because China will continue to advance with or without U.S. tech. I agree that China plays dirty and does not follow the same rules, but we cannot let that fear stop us from competing. Jensen wants real competition. He wants to go head-to-head with China’s best companies because he believes his company and the U.S. will come out on top.\n\nIn tech, influence matters as much as capability. The U.S. holds power because its influence is everywhere, from financial systems like Visa and Mastercard to music, movies, and more. If China builds a new AI tech stack and makes it open source, the U.S. could lose that influence, regardless of how advanced its own technology is. Free often wins.\n\nChina is the only true competitor to the U.S., not countries in Africa or Southeast Asia. Many of those markets are fine with “good enough” solutions if they cost little or nothing. I understand why Jensen is frustrated. He is leading, but part of that lead comes from the government limiting his competitors. I agree with him that if this continues, it will not be good for the U.S. It might help in the short term, maybe six months while things stabilize. ut capitalism must be free to do its thing. No matter how ruthless.",

      "id": "UgxIWPaw4nql3sEoOAd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Patel doesn't understand his own analogy. In his analogy the US has the finest enriched uranium. Where he fails with it is he assumes China's doesn't have their own enriched uranium. To make the analogy better you have to acknowledge China has enriched uranium. China's enriched uranium isn't as good. Jensen is saying \"Sure they can just use more uranium to match our destructive yield.\" \n\nTheir chips on a per chip and per wattage point of view aren't as good. That doesn't mean they can't match our raw compute power. They just need to use more chips and more energy to do it. They've already demonstrated they can do that. So then why can't I (Jensen) sell them chips? The question of why make it easier for them is fair. It ignores how your goal of preventing China from surpassing you isn't predicated on them not having your chips. Jensen is saying to stay ahead of China requires things that aren't an export ban. We didn't become the AI leader by implementing export bans.",

    {
      "id": "Ugz9TB4xRcc9RvcDlfR4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Dwarkesh did a phenomenal job here. Jensen's arguments don't really make sense in regards to selling chips to China if you do actually want the US to win on AI. I think he got a bit pressed here and panicked, because Dwarkesh's questions were so sharp.\nI felt like Jensen spent a lot of time throwing possible reasons at the wall trying to figure out what would stick besides 'NVidia can make a lot of short-term money in China'. This makes a lot of his arguments contradictory.\n\nThe one example I'll really highlight because it makes no sense, is this:\nIf a Chinese AI app is good for America when it runs on Nvidia, why is it bad for America when it runs on Huawei? The app is Chinese in both cases.\n\n\nI also think that the history of China copying American companies and then kicking them out, like Tesla, is extremely consistent and Jensen should not be eager at all to go into China.\n\nJensen talks about telecom; let's talk about Cisco and Huawei:\nCisco entered China as the dominant global router maker. Huawei entered the market with products that were suspiciously similar. Cisco sued in 2003, and after months of denying wrongdoing, Huawei admitted an employee had copied 2% of the router operating software from Cisco. IEEE Spectrum Cisco later revealed that the case involved \"direct, verbatim copying of our source code, to say nothing of our command line interface, our help screens, our copyrighted manuals and other elements of our products.\" \nThe copying was so thorough that Huawei had copied Cisco software including the bugs in the program.\n\nCisco then won the case in court, but obviously, Huawei won all of the Chinese market share. Ever since, Cisco has been systematically excluded by the Chinese government, until today where they have essentially zero market share there.\n\nYou can look this up.\nCisco -> Huawei\nGoogle -> Baidu\nTesla -> BYD\n\nEven in chips, ASML just had a dispute where a Chinese chipmaker had broken an DUV device trying to disassemble and copy it. There's a standard process:\n-Invite over foreign companies\n-Copy everything as thoroughly as possible\n-Restrict the foreign company's market access and sponsor the Chinese competitor\n-Foreign company retreats from Chinese market\n\nI don't know why he's so eager to go into this market, and to me its the ultimate example of shortsighted profit maximization.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCJy1j0QBUrJTCaeV5XU6QhQ",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Jensen made good points. He said that China can already do it if they wanted to. There's no real lock-in into their ecosystem. They have abundant energy. Even if their node process is behind, since AI is an embarrassingly parallel process, you could just scale out with even higher number of chips and use up their abundant energy, to match Nvidia's output. Which is bad, because and I agree with him mostly, a lot of the AI advances come from better algorithmic advances. So, eventually their better algorithms and processes will be optimised for Chinese tech stack. That could be bad for Americans (not for the rest of us though). Researchers still complain that to run rapid experiments and discover new techniques, even that is compute-bound as of now. But by definition, they don't have a compute bottleneck any greater than America because of the aforementioned chip scale-out solution on top of their abundant energy. Hence, it is strictly worse to cut off China's supply.     {
      "id": "UgyA341l0jcKq6IO3Qt4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Jensen's argument has historical basis. The GAO found in 2002 that restricting semiconductor equipment exports to China was ineffective because Japanese and European firms kept selling, only ~2 generations behind state-of-the-art. Same story with satellites post-ITAR (Europe built an \"ITAR-free\" industry that now outcompetes us on price), machine tools (US makers wiped out, we now import from China), and drones (Turkey's Bayraktar, DJI's dominance). There's a historical pattern of unilateral controls accelerating indigenization in the target country while handing market share to allied competitors who aren't restricted. The revenue loss then starves US firms of the R&D budget that created the lead in the first place. You can debate whether AI chips are different because of military dual-use urgency, but dismissing Jensen as self-interested ignores a 40-year pattern.",
      "like_count": 25,
      "author_id": "UCCPNF6vXtUGuZbittnQQNDw",
      "author": "@wonilart8426",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nb7MNlk6hRkPZoYav3aUshShIn788idkSD58uEakELxo8=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "1 day ago",
      "timestamp": 1776470400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyA341l0jcKq6IO3Qt4AaABAg.AVfUNDwAfC_AVhDvcvITtA",
      "parent": "UgyA341l0jcKq6IO3Qt4AaABAg",
      "text": "Exactly, Jensen understands Chinese history better than most: there is nothing China cannot build—it’s simply a matter of time. Paradoxically, restrictions only accelerate their self-reliance. Jensen’s core argument is that without these barriers, China would remain tied to global ecosystems; by cutting them off, the West is inadvertently forcing China to build its own domestic dominance.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCH6yD2baq94Ky9zv1IsrnPA",
      "author": "@zheouyang9884",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/xR0YRcirWzvadz0lO4j2mut99dFJIs2Mb79hAJIOJsjKlAwwo6YY7oqhB20q0Ri-ODEInmQF8w=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgyA341l0jcKq6IO3Qt4AaABAg",
      "text": "We’re going to base our trade policy on an industry analysis from 2002? Seriously? 😒 \nJapan produces a grand total of zero sub 4 nanometer semiconductors, same with the EU. Korea produces maybe 5% of global supply. Taiwan and the United States design and manufacture all of it. Period. The only way China gets sub 4nm chips is if we sell them to China. That’s it. So whatever the GAO thought in 2002 was in 2002. I was 8 years old in 2002.",

      "text": "This also misses the paramount importance of the tight timelines we’re dealing with right now.       "id": "Ugyp_ZdlWA13Jb4hPwJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Throughout the discussion regarding export controls and the competitive landscape for AI chips, Jensen Huang uses several strong, descriptive terms to push back against certain arguments or characterize specific viewpoints he disagrees with. \r\n\r\nChildish (1:21:56): Used to describe arguments that operate on extreme, \"zero or infinity\" premises regarding the impact of providing compute to China.\r\nLunacy (1:17:36): Used to characterize the comparison of AI technology to \"enriched uranium\" and the implications of selling chips for export.\r\nTorturous (7:15): Used to describe the dense, educational nature of his keynotes where he feels compelled to explain complex supply chain dynamics.\r\nLousy (1:17:50, 1:17:51): Used twice to dismiss the \"enriched uranium\" analogy as an illogical and ineffective way to frame the AI chip situation.\r\nNarrow-minded (1:25:40): Used to critique policies he believes are overly focused on immediate restrictions without considering the long-term unintended consequences for American industry leadership.\r\nHorrible (1:33:32): Used to describe the potential outcome of creating two disconnected, global ecosystems where one is built entirely on a foreign tech stack.",

      "text": "Dwarkesh may be framing questions in as plain as terms as he can manage for his audience, but unfortunately it also overlaps with the typical sensationalist journalism tactics of misrepresenting the situation as more simplistic and controversial than necessary.       "id": "UgwFgYC_IYy0WNPysHt4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Jensen seems to be making the point that if we have a policy of trying to 1) boycott part of the market for our models with our standards instead of 2) trying to dominate it with our models with our standards, then 3) we assure that those who we have boycotted will develop means to serve that market with their own models with their own standards resulting 4) in creating an entrenched competitor who not only will stand between us ever getting that portion of the market back but 5) also facing future losses of the market we already had, especially 6) as the competitor our boycott created will not be boycotting our share of the market but instead 7) will be ever more able to vigorously seek to take more and more parts of our self-truncated market for itself, 8) leaving us in numerous ways at an increasingly relatively reduced base for competitive developmental advances.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The mainstream tech community is currently hypnotized by the most lucrative silicon illusion in history. Praising legacy graphics processors for brute-forcing matri multiplication is like praising a slot machine for simulating a calculator. It is algorithmic mimicry packaged as a marketing fairytale, banking entirely on the general market's lack of hardware architecture knowledge. Transformers running on repurposed gaming chips are not exhibiting true artificial intelligence they are merely rendering a high-latency, statistical simulation bottlenecked by memory walls. True, zero-shot emergent cognitive properties require native tensor frameworks, not a rigged GPU trying to mimic an organic neural pathway. The moment investors wake up and realize they’ve been sold a brute-force abstraction layer instead of authentic computational architecture, this entire hardware bubble is going to correct itself in a single afternoon.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "The mainstream tech community is currently hypnotized by the greatest silicon illusion of the decade. People are praising legacy graphics processors (GPUs) for brute-forcing matrix multiplication and confusing it with actual emergent intelligence. It is algorithmic mimicry packaged as a marketing gimmick. Transformers running on these repurposed gaming cards are not AI they are just high-latency, static statistical simulations bottlenecked by memory walls.\nTrue zero-shot emergent properties,the actual architectural evolution that mimics unconstrained cognitive learning,require native tensor frameworks, not a rigged slot machine trying to simulate a brain. The moment investors and developers wake up and realize they’ve been sold a brute-force abstraction layer instead of actual neural architecture, this entire hardware bubble is going to correct itself in a single afternoon.       "id": "UgzQG7XCS6r-SHMZ7cx4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Dwarkesh has fine points, but he needs to read more history. His opinions are heavily short-sighted, as if science and engineering just stop (not really his fault, it's definitely the fault of fear mongering (and therefore parochial) of American politics and American AI companies), and Jensen is 100000% correct at macro scale. Jensen is also smart enough to be nuanced, and recognize that the final answer, is we have to both cooperate and compete instead of being anti-competitive. This was consistently the best answer throughout the 1900s, and anything else led to war or a cold war.\n\nIf you try to be anti-competitive with the world’s 2nd super power on key layers, you’re forcing them to innovate in a way that risks them leap frogging us and shutting us out long term only to create a new era of Chinese dominance. Sure if China was weak enough, you could bottle up science and engineering via embargo, but they're not. They have a young generation of hungry, driven, and brilliant working class that is an absolute behemoth built on a government that has issues, but at least uses it's wealth to take care of its people. Building on Nvidia almost slows down their chip layer innovation.\n\nThe question isn't \"if\" China starts to make headway on sub 7nm chips and starts to encroach on NVIDIA, it's when, and when they do we lose everything. Not giving them access to NVIDIA chips only emboldens them and paradoxically increases the chances of this. Building on NVIDIA means we share in technological innovations as a geopolitical system. It's literally an olive branch between the 2 actually functioning civilizations; a socialist autocracy and a capitalist (leaning socialist) democracy. Deng Xiaoping actually fixed China, and it should be clear whether we like it or not, that state run capitalism as an autocracy actually works. Yes there's less freedom for citizens compared to America and I think we should fight for democratic societies, their government actually takes care of their people swiftly unlike the increasingly non-functioning and over-indebted American government. We're smart enough to  learn from China, without just becoming a dictatorship. It's not like studying them magically turns us into a dictatorship. Stop it.\n\nEnriched uranium is actually a bad analogy from first principles. The level of enrichment you need to build WMD is far higher than what you need to create nuclear reactors. The type of plant you need to take fission level uranium to WMD uranium, would be as much as simply having the plant to go all the way in the first place. I’m surprised Jensen didn’t bring this up, and surprised Dwarkesh didn’t either. The difference is that we should trade resources with china (chips) and not actual weapons (unrestricted Mythos models). The amount of science and engineering it takes to go from chips to dangerous models is as big as it is to make the chips. We should always be ahead, and we should also trade resources responsibly without fear mongering.\n\nObviously we shouldn’t give them 100% of chips, but 0% is also a mistake, and I think that’s Jensen’s point which he made painfully clear only for Dwarkesh to 10000% fucking miss for like 30 minutes straight. \"We aren’t fucking losers\" That shit gave me chills when he said that. Jensen for president",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The idea that Mythos is this uniquely dangerous capability that can only occur at very high compute capacities is Anthropic marketing spin. Existing models, even quite small ones, with a small amount of fine tuning and a decent harness (neither of which demand heavy compute) could definitely launch effective attacks on the vast majority of important systems out there. The cybersecurity fence just isn't that high and security professionals have been warning about it for years. I'm absolutely certain that offensive Qwens and Gemmas are already out there and if they're not, it wouldn't be hard to make them. Mythos is probably the SotA but you mostly don't need SotA if you want a \"cyberweapon\" at this point",

    {
      "id": "UgzMn8uSAHgPTEWpTK94AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Highlights by TinaMind:\n00:32 NVIDIA 的核心價值在於從電子到運算單元（Tokens）的轉換過程，這需要極高的工程、科學與發明能力，並非單純的硬體製造，因此難以被輕易商品化。\n01:50 NVIDIA 採取「做必要的事，但盡可能少做」的策略，透過建立龐大的生態系統與上下游夥伴合作，將 NVIDIA 的架構打造為 AI 產業運作的基礎。\n21:01 CUDA 生態系統與靈活的程式編寫架構是 NVIDIA 的護城河，允許研究人員開發新演算法，這遠比單純的張量處理單元（TPU）更具彈性與市場擴展性。\n30:41 面對能源限制與硬體需求，NVIDIA 透過極端軟硬體協同設計與不斷迭代的架構，確保其產品始終維持最佳的總體擁有成本（TCO）與能效比。\n01:00:23 針對人工智慧的安全性與地緣政治，黃仁勳認為持續推動開放模型與全球技術對話，讓各國在美國技術堆疊上進行開發，是確保 AI 正向發展的最有效方式。\n01:15:53 強調必須維持美國在 AI 領域的領先地位，並確保美國實驗室優先獲得算力資源。\n01:16:40 黃仁勳主張不應放棄中國市場，認為這對美國科技領導地位及生態系發展不利，且應追求在產業鏈各層面皆贏。\n01:17:51 討論關於 AI 模型可能被用於開發網絡攻擊武器，以及針對高效能運算晶片的出口管制問題。\n01:20:49 說明 NVIDIA 的 CUDA 生態系具有深厚護城河，難以被輕易取代，這也是其持續創新的競爭關鍵。\n01:40:42 即使沒有 AI，NVIDIA 仍會致力於推動領域專用加速運算，以突破通用計算效能不足的瓶頸。",

      "id": "UgyCA8ZwORRAX0ZAjj14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Wow!  The temperature got hot in this interview.  Why?  Because Dwarkesh kept hammering at a real hot button for Jensen: the concession of the entire Chinese (and ultimately world) market to China due to concerns over safety.  My analysis: Jensen is correct that: a) open source is the future, b) AI success depends the whole stack (“5 layer cake”), c) export restrictions will result in the (open source) world using China’s stack, d) the US risks losing AI control to China as a result, and e) this would be a terrible outcome for the USA.\r\nHowever, Jensen’s fear of a - e (not to mention the economic hit that conceding the China market will cause to Nvidia)  has made him reluctant to acknowledge the real dangers that next-gen AI systems, like Mythos, pose.  An engineer should know you can’t solve a problem unless you acknowledge it first.  Safety concerns are real and getting bigger.  The answer is not to deny that they exist, or minimize them, but rather to get ahead of them – just as Nvidia does with every other engineering problem.  AI safety – properly done -- is a design and engineering problem.  No one does engineering better than Nvidia.  It’s time to step up.  I say this as someone who is a huge fan and stockholder of NVDA.",

      "text": "This wasn't a good episode for Dwarkesh because Jensen was making one point and Dwarkesh kept on assuming something else. Jensen was making a case about the important role public policy plays on national interests on energy infrastructure and import strategy while Dwarkesh kept on basing his knowledge on the idea that China will get ahold of AI on the application level making cyber attacks. \n\nDwarkesh did not have the background knowledge in order to carry out the conversation at his guest's level. Dwarkesh should have been briefed before the interview that open source inference libraries like xLLM has come to the scene, which is a open source Chinese-made inference engine that aims to compete with vLLM but targeted to Huawei's hardware. Dwarkesh also should have introduced his audience to the fact that the latest version of GLM 5.1 and DeepSeek v4 are no longer open source and are running closed source optimized on Chinese hardware. It's probably Jensen's fault not having his company's public relations set up this interview with the background context as a requirement to the publication of this episode.\n\nI felt like Dwarkesh exposed his age and generational gap between himself and Jensen. Jensen came in with a particular America-first view that he assumed would represent the U.S., but I think Dwarkesh still lacks a nationalistic identity to his show representing the U.S. the way Jensen assumed Dwarkesh would have a certain maturity in his political standing. \n\nWhen Dwarkesh could not keep up with the conversation, he should have paused the interview, gotten the necessary context, then continued once both of them have recovered after being on the same page. Instead this interview seemed like it was released in haste, and if he respected Jensen, would have edited it differently and kept the conversation going until they were on the same page, when I felt like they never quite got there due to Dwarkesh projecting his own experiences into Jensen's point without ever harnessing the awareness that he was doing so.",

    {
      "id": "UgwFd88segvDtchTGlB4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I loved the heated debate, it’s definitely clear that selling chips to China versus not selling chips to China both have advantages and disadvantages. Selling chips to China: Pro: Chinese chipmakers will make a lot less money competing with Nvidia, and are much less likely to have the capital necessary to build there own EUV. Con: China will have more compute then they would otherwise. Not selling chips to China is just flipping those two arguments, and I think that I agree more with Jensen on this point. Being afraid of China being able to mess us up is pretty stupid in my opinion, at any moment China could destroy the entire US with their nuclear weapons arsenal. Even just in the AI realm Jensen is entirely right that China will develop their own AI cyberattack capabilities regardless of how much compute that they have, sure they might not be as advanced as the US’s capabilities, but when we continue to use 30 year old software and 60 year old encryption techniques the question isn’t if China will develop this weapons it’s when. I think that delaying China somewhat is a good thing, but harming US chip manufacturing in the long term to delay China by 5-7 years instead of 2-4 years doesn’t make any sense to me, China developing their own chip making is the absolute worst case scenario for the United States (which is why we have the export controls on the ASML EUV machines in the first place). China is not Iran, we cannot prevent them from getting weapons that could cause major harm to the United States, not without starting WW3 and likely a nuclear holocaust given that as I already stated they already have the capability to do us serious harm. \nOn a final note, previous guests have stated concern around individuals having access to bioweapons and other AI powered weapons that could cause incredible harm and possibly kill millions of people, so it’s frankly ridiculous to say that an individual could do that and an entire nation of Chinas wealth and technological expertise couldn’t destroy the US.       "text": "We should go full steam ahead on technology infrastructure, because that's finite you can't copy and paste a physical data center, not yet anyway, but I guess you could wonder if we aren't actually helping other nations develop their technology faster any time we make a break through, that tends to be how innovation works, as some as someone anywhere figures something out, everyone else in the world inevitably figures that out, that's why dark forces have been going around assassinating people making discoveries, it's the only way to contain it, we've been held back from progressing, ideas that are becoming mainstream now, some people had a long time ago, but they mysterious vanished,\n\nit's harder to contain now because of the internet, me posting online wasn't just to bring attention to myself for personal gain, I've been doing it to leave a record, to protect myself, that if I was to suddenly stop posting, it would be suspicious, to create a deterence to taking me out because it would only spread my ideas further, the threats have been there they've basically told me they're going to kill me they want to take me out for uncovering things, they tried to pin the blame of destroying the universe onto me, painting me as that sort of threat, \n\nI guess that's why I have intentionally not gone into formal research, I probably would be dead, I decided to do it this way because it leaves room for doubt, because I don't definitely know there's room for doubt, people are free to dismiss what I hypothesize about, if I had actually proven what I suggest I might be dead,",

      "text": "1:13:26 \"If they're built on the American tech stack, how would that prevent them, if they have more advanced capabilities, from launching the Mythos-equivalent cyber attacks?\"\n\nI would say it wouldn't prevent them, but America would be able to catch up faster if tech stack remains the same.\nIf tech stacks diverge, any preparation efforts would fall flat and either side couldn't as easily copy each other.\n\nI think Patel has a point, compute is the main bottleneck that allows America to stay ahead in addition to algorithms that are mostly open source anyways. \nBut Huang also has a very good point, because different tech stacks would be problematic for stability and security.       "text": "​​ @aronchai  \"Any system on Earth\" is misinformed bullshit. Most widespread systems is not every system. I guess you learned to jump between extremes from Dwarkesh.       "text": "​ @RIURIU4  You're missing the point. The point is that even if chip export controls are a bad idea and it's net good and worthwhile to allow Nvidia to sell chips to China (as there is good reason to believe may be true, e.g. see the Dean Ball x Daniel Kokotajlo Anti-Debate in which the two agree on this point), the uranium analogy still holds. This is because all that is needed for the uranium analogy to be valid is for AI to be a dual-use technology, which it clearly is. You can easily hold the view that \"Yes, AI chips are analogous to uranium, because they can both be used for both good and bad purposes, but China isn't so bad, such that the costs associated with China having marginally more powerful dual-use chips are relatively small compared to the benefits of allowing the chip sales to China.\" In other words, there are a number of ways Jensen could have objected to Dwarkesh's argument against selling chips to China without rejecting the obviously valid analogy that AI chips are like uranium in that they are both dual-use. That's why Jensen's rejection of the analogy was crazy: it makes him look unreasonable and biased in general and there was absolutely no need for him to risk that since there were much better arguments he could have made to defend his position instead.",

      "id": "UgyhPt5DhlYZQ76yqD14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "32:50 This is total BS. InferenceMAX does not test the kind of systems-level TCO that Google is striving to obtain. As Google is not in the business of selling isolated TPU chips directly, I don't see what this would usefully reveal. \n\nIt's very nearly the most outrageous claim in tech history that Google could have saved a single dollar using Jensen's chips, rather than their homebrew solution. Moreover, without their homebrew TPUs to bring some discipline to the marketplace, Jensen's prices would be another 20% higher, across the board. \n\nJensen is using some kind of giant accounting fiction here where he assumes that most corporations purchasing this caliber of AI inference chip face difficulty in writing off the NRE of developing their own stack (rather than purchasing it externally) against their ongoing scale of operation. Google runs at a scale that poses almost NO difficulty in writing off their internal NRE. Owning their own stack is only going to get cheaper as agentic AI continues to advance. \n\nJensen is also leaning on a giant accounting fiction of TCO having a singular time horizon. Controlling your own ownership cost function is a major component of retaining freedom to innovate within a changing landscape. What TCO do you slap on that term? I would pretty much assign: priceless. \n\nFurthermore, Anthropic will soon replace the entire Nvidia developer community with a swarm of AI agents, which can quickly transfer the technology onto any suitable execution fabric.",

      "text": "Logline Timestamps\n- 0:00 — Electrons to tokens: why AI commoditization won't kill Nvidia\n- 1:46 — Nvidia's core philosophy: electrons in, tokens out — do as much as needed, as little as possible\n- 2:46 — Contrarian view: AI agents will cause software tool usage to skyrocket, not collapse\n- 4:26 — Nvidia's supply chain moat: $250B in commitments and how Jensen personally educates upstream CEOs\n- 8:32 — Can the upstream keep up? 2x annual growth is hitting TSMC's N3 capacity ceiling\n- 9:38 — Bottlenecks solve themselves: how the industry swarmed CoWoS packaging in two years\n- 13:04 — The hardest bottleneck isn't chips — it's plumbers, electricians, and energy policy\n- 16:23 — GPUs vs TPUs: why accelerated computing's flexibility beats specialization\n- 20:00 — The matrix multiply argument for TPUs and Jensen's programmability rebuttal\n- 22:00 — How Blackwell achieved 50x over Hopper without relying on Moore's Law\n- 24:43 — Does CUDA matter when hyperscalers write their own kernels?\n- 27:34 — The real CUDA moat: hundreds of millions of installed GPUs across every cloud\n- 29:17 — Nvidia's deep engineering teams routinely deliver 2-3x       "text": " @aronchai  You're twisting his arguments. He said that China can already do it if they wanted to. There's no real lock-in into their ecosystem. They have abundant energy. Researchers still complain that to run rapid experiments and discover new techniques, even that is compute-bound as of now. But by definition, they don't have a compute bottleneck any greater than America because of the aforementioned chip scale-out solution on top of their abundant energy.       "parent": "Ugwh1rlxuRaws9xtkjF4AaABAg",
      "text": "He actually does not do a great job with the explanation. He's trying to explain that his tech stack needs the networking effect for it to develop at maximum speed, but calls it an \"ecosystem\" instead. He also completely disregards the fact that China is a bad actor for whom IP laws don't mean anything and who will steal your technology. Once it gets an edge it will then put full state resources behind exploiting it, like they tried with the EVs but were stopped by tariffs. By selling China AI accelerators you're selling your mortal enemy the rope they will hang you with, while haggling for the best price. It's like selling the building blocks of the Manhattan Project to Hitler or Hirohito because \"we need the ecosystem\". When has an ecosystem infiltrated by bad actors benefited the creators?",

      "text": "​ @Notabotreally  Thank you.       "text": "I don't think the rest of the world can tolerate Jensen's ambitions much longer: RAM shortages, SSD shortages, HDD shortages, GPU shortages, the forced push to the cloud, and the lack of enough electricity and an overworked electrical grid — the world and the US just can't accommodate his expansionist dreams.",

      "text": "High prices are indicative of high demand. They did cover that perspective in the episode; I think that barring major geopolitical disruptions, NVidia works with its partners to always be targetting the weakest link. \n\nAnd this POV that RAM, SSD, HDD, GPU are in short supply is a purely relative to demand. In absolute terms, the rate at which of each of these goods is being produced is only accelerating. \n\nIt's just that consumers are being priced out of the hardware market at the moment. But real prices only stay high in the short-run. My primary fear is in regard to large geopolitical disruption.",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mTpPRhR-rx-STdrdSZTXDoiWU7WQmCb5SyUfIudJ6gMPjoCU22-s9sP64I6dhIMCzjPw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgyjDmG3-QSpaJYMWGt4AaABAg.AVdDWtzOmIrAVdFc-AQADV",
      "parent": "UgyjDmG3-QSpaJYMWGt4AaABAg",
      "text": "I believe his argument goes like this: \n\n1 - If given the option, Chinese firms will choose the best and most abundant stack on which to build, which is Nvidia. \n2 - without that option, they will choose the only other option they have, which is to build their own. \n\nI think that he makes the argument in a number of different ways that this is a nuanced issue. Making chips is hard but not impossible, so if givne the choice, no producer in China would choose to do what NVidia is doing because competing against them is a fool's errand. However, if NVidia is locked out of the Chinese ecosystem, then they would not have to compete against them, so there will be producers who choose to do what Nvidia does, within the Chinese ecosystem.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCQR1bV9Td89IsGPY0qsQgnw",
      "author": "@OneDerscoreOneder",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nrm-LSQT7Bt9D3mF_6QTDwa1JZDFOwWb16TeWz1jIpWSjR=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgxVkMX9sgJ-Fc2T3AZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Jensen got nailed here and he knew he was just saying he wants personal benefit for his company. The decision to provide compute to a country with unlimited energy we are done.",
      "like_count": 25,
      "author_id": "UCVawwGZ1gkFcPhCa0u9ug4Q",
      "author": "@DolbyS-u8z",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lq_ys0z-F8TY71iMY238mtSI7xHTtIfK5xpj_ArOwQ_Y1a86jQgSV_wej4oKrByN5fYQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgxVkMX9sgJ-Fc2T3AZ4AaABAg.AVdDWiSduYxAVdH0EDTfXf",
      "parent": "UgxVkMX9sgJ-Fc2T3AZ4AaABAg",
      "text": "There is nothing stopping chinese firms from buying American tokens. I believe that is what he means by \"every layer of the stack is important.\" The 5 layers to which he is referring are these: \n\n\"Energy — AI needs massive power to run data centers and training workloads.\n\nChips — GPUs and other accelerators provide the compute.\n\nCloud infrastructure — Networking, orchestration, and data-center systems connect and manage the compute.\n\nModels — The foundation models that learn from data and generate outputs.\n\nApplications — The products that turn AI into real economic value, like copilots, robotics, and drug discovery tools.\"\n\n\n\nHe is arguing that in trying to win the model race, we are giving up the infrastructure and chip race, which are arguably more important. And if you lose the chip and cloud then you probably also will lose the application layer. \n\n If you believe that tokens are a comparatively fungible resource (which I personally do), then that would make it the least important layer out of the 5 in the long-run. He argues that if you force China to create their own vertical integration, that it will strengthen them in the long run. Something they would not do unless they were forced to do so. \n\n\n\nHe also alludes to a similar protectionist measure that was taken during Trump 1, which stifled US telecom growth in 2019. Here is Claude's explanation of the telecom example: \n\"The Huawei ban is perhaps the sharpest illustration of Huang's \"unintended consequences\" argument. In 2019, the US placed Huawei on its Entity List, barring American companies from supplying it with goods, technology, or intellectual property — the security rationale being that China's 2017 Intelligence Law compels Chinese companies to cooperate with state intelligence services on demand, making Huawei-built infrastructure a potential backdoor into critical networks. The problem was that by 2019, the US had no meaningful domestic telecom equipment industry left. Lucent had collapsed and been absorbed by French Alcatel. Nortel had gone bankrupt. Motorola had sold its network division. So when the ban took effect, it didn't redirect contracts to American companies — it redirected them to Ericsson and Nokia, a Swedish and a Finnish firm. The policy successfully neutralized Huawei as a security threat inside the US, which was its stated goal, but it did nothing to establish American control over telecom infrastructure. The US ended up dependent on allied-but-foreign vendors, having neither a Chinese competitor nor an American one. A policy framed around national security arguably left the nation's infrastructure no more sovereign than before.\n\n\"",

      "author_id": "UCQR1bV9Td89IsGPY0qsQgnw",
      "author": "@OneDerscoreOneder",

    {
      "id": "UgzC2oHO9NrsHLDblud4AaABAg.AVdCpj_EQt9AVdHHoCZ4M1",
      "parent": "UgzC2oHO9NrsHLDblud4AaABAg",
      "text": "There is nothing stopping chinese firms from buying American tokens. I believe that is what he means by \"every layer of the stack is important.\" The 5 layers to which he is referring are these: \n\n\"Energy — AI needs massive power to run data centers and training workloads.\n\nChips — GPUs and other accelerators provide the compute.\n\nCloud infrastructure — Networking, orchestration, and data-center systems connect and manage the compute.\n\nModels — The foundation models that learn from data and generate outputs.\n\nApplications — The products that turn AI into real economic value, like copilots, robotics, and drug discovery tools.\"\n\n\n\nHe is arguing that in trying to win the model race, we are giving up the infrastructure and chip race, which are arguably more important. And if you lose the chip and cloud then you probably also will lose the application layer. \n\n If you believe that tokens are a comparatively fungible resource (which I personally do), then that would make it the least important layer out of the 5 in the long-run. He argues that if you force China to create their own vertical integration, that it will strengthen them in the long run. Something they would not do unless they were forced to do so. \n\n\n\nHe also alludes to a similar protectionist measure that was taken during Trump 1, which stifled US telecom growth in 2019. Here is Claude's explanation of the telecom example: \n\"The Huawei ban is perhaps the sharpest illustration of Huang's \"unintended consequences\" argument. In 2019, the US placed Huawei on its Entity List, barring American companies from supplying it with goods, technology, or intellectual property — the security rationale being that China's 2017 Intelligence Law compels Chinese companies to cooperate with state intelligence services on demand, making Huawei-built infrastructure a potential backdoor into critical networks. The problem was that by 2019, the US had no meaningful domestic telecom equipment industry left. Lucent had collapsed and been absorbed by French Alcatel. Nortel had gone bankrupt. Motorola had sold its network division. So when the ban took effect, it didn't redirect contracts to American companies — it redirected them to Ericsson and Nokia, a Swedish and a Finnish firm. The policy successfully neutralized Huawei as a security threat inside the US, which was its stated goal, but it did nothing to establish American control over telecom infrastructure. The US ended up dependent on allied-but-foreign vendors, having neither a Chinese competitor nor an American one. A policy framed around national security arguably left the nation's infrastructure no more sovereign than before.\n\n\"",

      "id": "UgzBMXTGFeHX49rZ5OF4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Let's play out the future outcome where NVIDIA is banned from selling in China. The future is not just the next few years, it's the next 20, the next 50. \n\n1) Huawei will dominate chip manufacturing. If you disagree, you do not understand China and the Chinese people. \n2) Researchers in China will start using Huawei technology stack and optimize for that instead of NVIDIA. \n3) Chinese models out of China start to outpace models in USA, a likely scenario - look at how many Chinese researchers are in China and in the USA. It's almost all of them.\n4) If you want the best model, you have to buy Huawei.\n\nCongratulations you just gave away your country's competitive advantage in chips and now forced everyone in USA to buy Huawei technology. But actually, they won't sell it to you, only to NK and Russia, or maybe they do sell to you and now to have to buy Chinese AI infrastructure. That is not winning.\n\nI also want to emphasize that the usage of analogies, any analogy, is generally incorrect. If the two things being compared in an analogy were actually so similar, then they would be the same thing and no anology would be needed. Analogies often fail because they compare two different things that each have their own nuances that are lost with a simplistic comparison.\n\nThe next point is that AI won't just be used to find zero days. AI in a few years will be capable of so much more than zero days. The threat and attack surface of a godlike AI cannot be predicted. We might as well bomb them now if the argument is that we cannot let China get their hands on a powerful AI. Selling chips to them is so low on pole of priorities of how to address this future reality. Whether we sell to them or not today will not affect whether China will achieve godlike AI. They will, with or without NVIDIA chips. This is a marathon and the world is not ending in 3 years. Banning NVIDIA from China determines whether or not NVIDIA gets to be part of that future.",

      "text": "Why Jensen is so angry? He got triggered to simple question?",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCwJMBXdnH_QXXMg-ADTB-Yg",
      "author": "@meghrajairekar",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kxfVx00aidU5jq39z41U3_nMoWRAcWKFpyPysBBGmaQKc=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "_time_text": "2 days ago",
      "timestamp": 1776384000,
      "is_pinned": false

    {
      "id": "Ugx9ua8Jf1jpMCdxW0B4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Once you force a country  to develop tech like to make chips, they will develop this tech. Eventually they may beet us at this game. If they can buy our chips, maybe their effort to in-house will be delayed.\nJessen makes a valid point.",
      "like_count": 5,
      "author_id": "UCqdS2jkrPYhp16oHU8ArZHA",
      "author": "@johngrabner",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n45Ah2aArs40rCTw4naWt2EVbgNktQeh2pyXIztZp6AdY=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 days ago",
      "timestamp": 1776384000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugx9ua8Jf1jpMCdxW0B4AaABAg.AVd9gZ119bPAVdyS-wRaeZ",
      "parent": "Ugx9ua8Jf1jpMCdxW0B4AaABAg",
      "text": "Jensen is wrong.  China has every intention of being self-sufficient in all significant technologies regardless of international relations.  The effect of Jensen's policy is simply to accelerate China's progress in developing AI models.  It is a dead loser for the West.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCZJ2eWwnM3VDiHBuuFgS3qQ",
      "author": "@kreek22",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lyYgO-icPiGtAUInENxlFvNvbSkhIvtme5qh-feNA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "author_is_verified": false,

      "_time_text": "2 days ago",

      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugx9ua8Jf1jpMCdxW0B4AaABAg.AVd9gZ119bPAVdMHct0U9_",
      "parent": "Ugx9ua8Jf1jpMCdxW0B4AaABAg",
      "text": "It is only half-valid since it does not matter who has more computing power -despite his fear mongering marketing.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UChQzM5250pwJ6yWjuDLVTZw",
      "author": "@c-lipps",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/wELkz9n1VqMCahIHNZWNfJTEDzuK35SCzdgVO4LkidK7RM1-AVTIymxBq5W451s5NQSjBKTgGw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "Ugx9ua8Jf1jpMCdxW0B4AaABAg.AVd9gZ119bPAVdMHct0U9_",
      "text": " @c-lipps so he’s not suppose to market for his business. Get out of here with that childish mindset",

      "author_id": "UCvnjkTPD5ZG_q0G6H_dlVYw",
      "author": "@JimMcNutty",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kexSU46w6cYLAw7n2skj-kjy6uv4tRLz7Q3K1rsh5kWb6z0DWyfRdUElppkPxsBgt36Q=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    },
    {
      "id": "Ugx9ua8Jf1jpMCdxW0B4AaABAg.AVd9gZ119bPAVdgATdBzvl",
      "parent": "Ugx9ua8Jf1jpMCdxW0B4AaABAg",
      "text": "And it makes them dependent on us. I mean, China manufactures a ton of products for us. Why? It makes us dependent. It'd be foolish not to do the same.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCzqAQuiXWZJrDKiqJYXzB9Q",
      "author": "@someguy3186",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l8e4GdyniCECnjATYgVtwMNTAR8ODmvYBImaoyV5I=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugz-zd8LgZqxMqLYDPZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I like seeing the fired up Jensen. You read about it and so many who work for him have stories about him dressing down employees no matter who is listening. Well done, Dwarkesh. You stood your ground and brought out the best in your guest. Excellent episode.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCVHBZFd7y6M_nb5fuqbfLuw",
      "author": "@KyleEstle",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_ksQQl2B9h3YStUGVnbkEBwQ17nquLWhFzYP0HbtW3Fg4xF0T91e_MyLGpXuaKOx1LlOQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 days ago",

      "is_pinned": false

    {
      "id": "UgwBNu0Q1j0vdY2Dmx94AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Obviously, better computation + better brain will win the battle. However, why battle?  Why not cooperate instead and focus on making a better life, enhancing humanity?",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCGat5eSpn9NHxZfT0g1YkCQ",
      "author": "@cyberinstalledquantum",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/48HH8O4orIbPjIeAKJ1f3hKxuIm3JEsjaodRvgqqYZlrP3_u7Uss8vj7GWmkAFYDDZObqjQWYPk=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,

      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 days ago",
      "timestamp": 1776384000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwBNu0Q1j0vdY2Dmx94AaABAg.AVd9_SJ3Q_0AVdAwHlKNqG",
      "parent": "UgwBNu0Q1j0vdY2Dmx94AaABAg",
      "text": "We worked and gave everything to them for four decades. We now know their intentions, hence the posturing. You’re just ignorant to the history.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCTAMcMUO7YGzc0j3FHWC0Qw",
      "author": "@Likeaworm",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mvi3Wkp4T65PYPFNFMHC4S8L0jtVo7RIBSrvKjeEM=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgwBNu0Q1j0vdY2Dmx94AaABAg.AVd9_SJ3Q_0AVdAwHlKNqG",
      "text": " @Likeaworm I might not know the history but I am afraid that they will be better than us. I sincerely have to admit that they have very smart people, I worked with few of those smart people. What if one day they are better than us, then what? Are we going to beg for their technology? I hope not and I root for the U.S. 100%, but we don’t know what the future holds. To me, cooperation makes more sense than competition.",

      "author_id": "UCGat5eSpn9NHxZfT0g1YkCQ",
      "author": "@cyberinstalledquantum",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/48HH8O4orIbPjIeAKJ1f3hKxuIm3JEsjaodRvgqqYZlrP3_u7Uss8vj7GWmkAFYDDZObqjQWYPk=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I respect Dwarkesh for pushing his questions, but I think he got fixated on the hardware layer of the stack and using Mythos as the only counter example. It made sense to me when Jensen explained that the other layers like energy, applications etc. are where it's going to make the most difference in this AI race.",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kV4K57zC8kYKlSY__LaaXb3PJI8SlhNc7W4385Ayvl6Zo=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgxjFBiD-N4ZsSWRETZ4AaABAg",
      "text": "Not really. Dwarkesh was right. Dwarkesh didn't have an opinion, as he said at the start of the discussion. And he was playing devils advocate. He was disagreeing with Jensen refusing to see the cost and danger.\n\nBiggest mistake US national security was for Apple and US big tech give their know how to China. Important question.",

      "author_id": "UCGGgnCAU6DoXY3BvpelFqag",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_laVs92NFbpObEsbEJYmyxxhpTkHLyt1BHyOd_9oHg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "​ @kindnesslove5482  You’re conflating building an ecosystem with assembling phones—they’re fundamentally different. The continued dominance of iOS and Android shows how difficult it is to develop a competitive alternative.       "text": "5:09 it's not hard for google!       "text": "We are the Swarm .     {

      "text": "@margorana2628 Cyberwarfare will happen regardless of diplomacy or not because they are our adversary.  What he is saying is that if there is going to be a \"winner\" in the future on which tech infrastructure AI is built on he prefers it to be built on American tech.  I don't understand how that could be a bad thing.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UChbnyzboV3opgGSc5ZuHhtQ",
      "author": "@coast2koast",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nSez7amJHSg-LxUd3k4RxwMKmzYUQXYn8-g0yv-8s=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgzJGnMjLTqumQx6I2h4AaABAg.AVd-b8dDp-pAVi8qud80cC",
      "parent": "UgzJGnMjLTqumQx6I2h4AaABAg.AVd-b8dDp-pAVgO0ko0CI6",
      "text": " @coast2koast  Here’s the reason that’s a bad idea: The gun that shoots you will kill you, regardless of whether or not it’s American steel.\n\nThe notion that the software or hardware being used were American would somehow limit China is a faulty thesis, because it doesn’t tell us at all HOW that would be the case. Do we have a kill switch that explodes all the GPUs in their labs? Is there a software throttle button? What is it? Without this point being clarified, the analogy of the gun and steel is actually 1:1.\n\nThe idea that Huang is giving is: they’re basically far away from it now. If I can sell them enough GPUs, they’ll switch to our framework, and we can decide to stop selling it to them when the race is getting close. Basically, we’re able to leverage them more because they’ve already committed to using American technology, and now that they’re locked in they would be killing time trying to reverse course and switch operating models to native-built ones.\n\nThere are many issues with this thesis. For one, they have such an advantage on energy and talent, that if we give them tech too, we have no way of predicting if they reach offensive capabilities first; we would be playing a dangerous all-in gambit.\nSecondly, what makes you think the Chinese would fall for Huang’s trap? They’re a centralized government. The Chinese aren’t stupid. They’d see what you’re doing and instead of allowing companies to build on NVIDIA systems, they’d block them from doing it until they could copy it, otherwise they’re obviously walking into a trap. And because they’re a centralized government, they can interfere with the private sector however they like. You’re basically giving them your homework and having them copy it. Like Tesla, Apple, and a bunch of other “smartest” American companies got played.\n\nThe issue isn’t whether or not a competitor will be building on American technology, the crux is that we do NOT want them to build it AT ALL—like, ever. Ideally, in a fantasy world, Xi would wake up and decide to destroy all of China’s AI infrastructure. Obviously that’s never going to happen, and the strategy here is: if you want it that bad, build it yourself… from scratch.\n\nHuang’s whole thesis is like saying, if the robber wants to break into the bank, he’ll find a way to the vault and break it, so we might as well leave the vault open.(--?!) No! If they want the money, let them work for it. If China wants AGI, let them build it from scratch, no helpsies. If they get there first?!—hey, fair enough. Let the best win.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCHII1M5kMxApBfe_GJdWubA",
      "author": "@yaboisartre5844",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/LNB7dziVjvjFfG4NBbw7sqMv84A_eMtkoKQ4ML-9znccG98jC70GlX_wYrHYc36-ywRz9p_gI_Y=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "17 hours ago",
      "timestamp": 1776456000,
      "is_pinned": false

      "parent": "UgzJGnMjLTqumQx6I2h4AaABAg.AVd-b8dDp-pAVgO0ko0CI6",
      "text": "​ @coast2koast Talking about \"winning\" and \"losers\" is about as shallow as that conversation could have gotten. His entire focus was on personal gain, not international interests and the safety of the United States - which is far more important than how much of a winner or loser he or his company ends up being - as someone deeply concern with the influence China is trying to exert over the world, I could not possibly care less about this man's company and ego.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCe5Coyj5QukrBi5_VYkku3g",
      "author": "@allrequiredfields",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l3RHchbvC8I1YeRZryfcwulaUrtDSTS27SEAWJ4JA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgzJGnMjLTqumQx6I2h4AaABAg.AVd-b8dDp-pAViitou69oJ",
      "parent": "UgzJGnMjLTqumQx6I2h4AaABAg.AVd-b8dDp-pAVgO0ko0CI6",
      "text": " @yaboisartre5844  By that logic, America should just roll over and surrender, given china have such an advantage on energy and talent as you claim, if we don't give them the tech they would just develop better tech themselves. Like how China couldn't get on the ISS and just made one themselves. The whole argument is, Nvidia sell the hardware, re-invest the money into better hardware so essentially china is funding Nvidia's research, instead of funding their own. Sure they will still fund their own research, but hopefully, Nvidia will improve its hardware at a higher speed given the additional investment. Why would you want china to have another ISS moment except with AGI now, you want a tightly knit relation to ensure mutual benefit.",

      "text": "​ @alaza78 @alaza78 It's not illegal to buy Chinese EVs in America, but I take your point; it is much more expensive and much more inconvenient due to tariffs and software incompatibilities. It's important to remember, however, that those were largely due to China not allowing American EVs to compete in Chinese markets in the first place, so it is a political response as much as everything else. \nThe point remains the same, though, America wins because of its excellence, not because of its punitive and restrictive practices. That is ultimately the key ingredient for long-term success. Spending time and energy restricting others is ultimately a losing game; we win by focusing on our own excellence, which we can control.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCLh-xYdSQFs7W5wyJcOstiw",
      "author": "@titovaldes",

      "text": " @titovaldes  He's right.  No one would buy them for a simple reason.  In America, the marginal shortage is energy and Chinese chips are much less energy efficient.  I'm not sure Huawei could give its chips to the major American AI companies for free.",

      "text": " @titovaldes  一、主要美系品牌累计销量（估算）\n通用汽车（含别克、雪佛兰、凯迪拉克、五菱）\n累计：约 5000 万辆\n峰值：2017 年 400 万辆\n2017 年后下滑，2024 年约 180 万辆\n福特（含长安福特、江铃福特、林肯）\n累计：约 1200 万辆\n峰值：2016 年 127 万辆\n2024 年：44.2 万辆\n特斯拉（2014 年入华）\n累计：约 450 万辆\n2022 年峰值：71 万辆\n2025 年：62.6 万辆\n其他（Jeep、克莱斯勒、道奇等）\n累计：约 300 万辆",

      "parent": "UgxfJdmzIVxH93ype3N4AaABAg.AVcuwrmjCk7AVd9tslaRgm",
      "text": " @Casino6789  this interview is so uncomfortable because dwarkesh is kinda rude but i think he's right. yea jensen cant be perfectly honestly but i think this is the real answer. \n\njensen: i am not going to lock out a massive market for nvidia just to slow down an inevitability that china will reach parity with the united states on ai technology. i will not fall on the sword for america. we're also not 100% sure that this thing that will hurt nvidia will actually work against china at all because they don't need to use these chips for chatbots. they don't need the massive compute required just to create a mythos like ai. even with their 7nm chips. they can scrape together enough of them to do it. on the other hand, we want them to be reliant on american tech stack so we might have some semblance of control over it later. \n\nfrom a purely geopolitical standpoint, yea dont sell chips to china. but america isnt a communist country and nvidia isnt the government, it's a private company that wants to make money. this isnt selling weapons grade plutonium to china, it's selling something that maybe will help them do something they would've already been able to do anyway.",

      "text": " @ScaredNerd more like If I go down because I can’t sell in China, Imma make sure everybody else goes down. But it’s a little weird and hypocritical that Jensen sees the Chinese market as essential while the US has banned Chinese hardware",

      "text": " @pianoforte611  My best guess is AI will be like the advent of the internet and the computer revolution combined. It will (eventually) be part of every single industry.
