      "text": "How is he not doing that? When do you think he fails to do what you're describing \n\nI thought he did very well. On the surface his tone may sound like he's merely referencing industry jargon and Jensen seems to partially treat as such, but most of what he's saying follows from careful premeditated thought & research - like are these not THE questions to ask?",

    {
      "id": "UgzUugLWkxyv2eJo6ad4AaABAg.AVcurLGgx5IAVd4RnIGreT",
      "parent": "UgzUugLWkxyv2eJo6ad4AaABAg.AVcurLGgx5IAVcvHdadxmm",
      "text": "​ @willwimbiscus7456 because he is seeing this as a race that the US must win. Win what? His core belief is that intelligence is unlocked only by hardware acceleration. That is verifiable false, you only have to look to the human brain that runs on 20w, and is materially slower than silicon for processing. So it's not a hardware issue, it's an information processing issue. Human brains only think 5-6 steps in sequence. AI can think 90-150 steps in sequence, but can't continuously move the frame of reference to decompose the problem from multiple angles at once.  \nThis has nothing to do with hardware, it is a information systems processing issue. \nThe hardware stack for a properly defined AI system that can think exactly the same way that we do is ALREADY significant overkill.  \nSo hardware protection is causing China to look at the actual bottleneck, which is the architecture of models.",

      "id": "Ugxu3KIXbr2J8W-EGVh4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "To summarize Jensen's argument: We should keep the USA ahead in semiconductor technology, but we should still compete in the Chinese markets. If Nvidia chips like Vera Rubin are better than Hopper, but even Hopper is better than the Huawei chips, then we should sell Hopper to China while using Vera Rubin for ourselves. Removing Nvidia from the Chinese markets gives additional incentive for them to improve their own tech stack (which they would do regardless, but probably not at the same rate) and to try to spread their competing tech stack around the world (which poses obvious risks, as seen with telecommunications).",

      "author_id": "UC1nm9ZWIzirxLBiLGJetrCw",
      "author": "@gunaysoni6792",

      "text": "Exactly, Jensen understands Chinese history better than most: there is nothing China cannot build—it’s simply a matter of time.       "text": "​ @An_Alien_Observing_Earthlings  do you honestly think that they don't already get their hands on the technology via black markets?\n\nIt's not a matter of technology access that prevents them from overtaking us, it's a skill and manpower issue.",

    {
      "id": "Ugxu3KIXbr2J8W-EGVh4AaABAg.AVcrC8ha4iVAVfa03Z7_IV",
      "parent": "Ugxu3KIXbr2J8W-EGVh4AaABAg",
      "text": "He also says China can just link its own chips but wants them in the US ecosystem. They’re not dependent on the US as bottleneck",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCZxho0Sb-4v17uoECZHn6EA",
      "author": "@IslamicRageBoy",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kH9KcfcMvvEY6d7P2ZQaQ4pH5qZYBy6rZq-ZpcvU1PWA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugxu3KIXbr2J8W-EGVh4AaABAg.AVcrC8ha4iVAVjDdP83Fk0",
      "parent": "Ugxu3KIXbr2J8W-EGVh4AaABAg",
      "text": "Technology does not improve in a vacuum. No amount of money or intelligence can foresee all the problems down the road. Successful technology emerges when it is widely used and benefits from extensive user feedback to identify bugs and request features. Take Linux and Android, for example.\n\nIf Chinese companies had access to cheaper and better U.S. technology, they would have little incentive to port their work to a different stack. Doing so is costly and time-consuming. As a result, a domestic Chinese stack struggles to improve quickly with a smaller user base. There is precedent for this: for years, China relied on U.S. chip design software from Cadence and Synopsys. It has its own alternatives, but few want to use them because they are inferior. They are inferior largely due to insufficient user feedback to guide improvements.\n\nThe current policy of restricting China’s access to U.S. technology has slowed its AI ambitions, but it also risks creating a rival that may eventually compete across the entire stack, rather than just at the application layer using U.S. hardware.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCNFE_nIAHG-izbupvSpJV9g",
      "author": "@Lore-mn2xx",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l1GafD9G2xUKk3DZXEIbjWqFYUKvlruSNnGqh3GlE=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "7 hours ago",
      "timestamp": 1776492000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "parent": "Ugxu3KIXbr2J8W-EGVh4AaABAg",
      "text": "I don't think the rate of Chinese insourcing will change at all no matter what the US does. They are not going to allow the US to hold a critical bottleneck over them",

      "author_id": "UCayenwbrOFwRdpsRS2F-HkQ",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nYPi4TjQFNzw-wjdGXGyPspWExmP3s6rl4TEDIy40vR_xQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": " @andrewpei9801  You can't point to how China responded to the chip bans as evidence of, see they were going to do it anyways. They're only doing it because they now have no choice, but before NVIDIA had 90% of market share in China, to say 'hey we were gonna lose that anyways' is loser mentality. Tesla still has sizable market share in China's EV market, even with BYD. Apple also has sizable market share in China, and neither company has regretted entering the market or are seeking to leave the market. And NVIDIA's CUDA ecosystem is much stickier than a car or a phone, that's the point Jensen was making. And for every dollar NVIDIA makes in the China market, they could plow back into R&D, making their chips better and fortifying their moat.",

      "text": "​ @DavidWilson-ux2ll  the argument from the other side is the illusion of ecosystem moat - platforms are open and China is often staying ahead or leading in some aspects of the research , and 2. illusion of trust between researchers - wherein there is some way to convince the CCP to not built against us - and Jensen's position is : \"USA will always be better\" - which is speculative at best, that is why Dwarkesh is concerned that outfitting an ideological competitor is counterintuitive to our long term competitive social standing..\n\nJensen needs to defend his shareholders - he can't concede profits, no matter where they come from.\n\nDwarkesh is also forgetting that AI is just one domain China has already developed and scaled industry beyond to what US has.",

      "text": "​ @thadiusbarnelsnatch3665  Nvidia is deeply embedded in the technology infrastructure of major American corporations.       "parent": "Ugxu3KIXbr2J8W-EGVh4AaABAg",
      "text": "All you have to do is reverse the names - if China was in the US position and the US was in China's position, the argument that China blocking tech transfer will be \"good for the US because the Americans would then invent their own tech stack\" would be laughed out of the room.  It would be wholly obvious that you don't give tech to an adversary.  The only reason why we make this argument is because it's bad for China for the US to finally put up blocks to their tech transfer, so to speak, so we have to invent double speak to make it seem like it's the opposite.",
      "like_count": 7,
      "author_id": "UC5qIm-kBDgECA8yvNRi2Kxw",
      "author": "@nishensemble",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mfuAj0rINJiDTzaVX5QlkkA3TZ4YoIbBEtBdldhso=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": " @nishensemble  \"It would be wholly obvious that you don't give tech to an adversary.\" Ok so then why do American AI frontier labs actively recruit Chinese AI researchers? If they're the enemy, why are we recruiting the Cold War equivalent of Russian nuclear scientists? Because it would cripple American AI labs if they weren't allowed to recruit the best AI researchers, most of which happen to be Chinese.",

      "text": " @TheOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO  Look I personally don't support the tariffs on Chinese EVs (because as a consumer I would be more than happy to buy cheap EVs) but the idea is that the tariffs create a temporary buffer for legacy automakers like Ford and GM to transition to EVs.     {
      "id": "Ugxz_EXOLlKxiGvxKml4AaABAg.AVcmhGuTR39AVecm7djKer",
      "parent": "Ugxz_EXOLlKxiGvxKml4AaABAg",
      "text": "I can prove that if Dwarkesh had used a \"good cop\" attitude rather than a \"bad cop\" one, he would have gotten a lot more important things out of Jensen today!\n\nDwarkesh is extremely smart and intelligent, but this episode shows the limits of his confrontational approach. True triggering will get out a guest's \"true colors,\" but a triggered man is also speaking out of ego and not just rational thinking.\n\nFor example, when Dwarkesh pushed him on whether Nvidia could sustain its margins against hyperscalers, Jensen immediately pivoted to a defensive 'F1 racer' analogy rather than a raw financial breakdown. If Dwarkesh had used a more collaborative approach, he might have gotten Jensen to talk about specific yield improvements or CoWoS packaging instead of 'experts' and 'losers.'\n\nYou can see the peak 'triggered' moment during the China debate when Jensen calls Dwarkesh’s premises ‘childish’ and even flatly tells him, ‘You are talking to the expert’.\n\nBy the end, Jensen is so focused on not looking like a 'loser' that the conversation becomes more about dominance than about the actual mechanics of the chip industry (like the physical bottlenecks of 7nm vs 3nm chips). It's highly entertaining, but as an technical viewer, I'd trade the heated clashes for that lost technical clarity any day!",

      "text": "At the same time, I think he takes the view \"everything is questionable\" too far and it has been amplified with the new AI era where it is believed that tribal knowledge is useless or that people who have them are no better than genz new grads and that is total bs. \n\nAnd you could see, at times Jensen reinforcing quite frustratingly to Dwarkesh on how he should trust Jensen blindly on his knowledge of the mechanics of semiconductor supply and the logistics when he says something with authority (as someone who has been in this industry for probably 40 years).       "parent": "Ugxz_EXOLlKxiGvxKml4AaABAg",
      "text": "I get what you’re saying, but I don’t think it’s just about “asking direct questions.” There’s a difference between pushing for clarity and framing things in a way that assumes the worst outcome.\r\n\r\nJensen’s point wasn’t that risks don’t exist, it’s that cutting off access doesn’t freeze progress, it just shifts it elsewhere. That’s the part people keep brushing past. You can’t regulate innovation globally by pretending one side will just stop.",

## Description

I asked Jensen about TPU competition, Nvidia’s lock on the ever more bottlenecked supply chain needed to make advanced chips, whether we should be selling AI chips to China, why Nvidia doesn’t just become a hyperscaler, how it makes its investments, and much more. Enjoy!

## Transcript

We've seen the valuations of a bunch of&nbsp; software companies crash because people&nbsp;&nbsp; are expecting AI to commoditize software. There's a potentially naive way of thinking&nbsp;&nbsp; about things, which is: look,&nbsp;

Nvidia sends a GDS2 file to TSMC.&nbsp; TSMC builds the logic dies, it builds the&nbsp; switches, then it packages them with the HBM&nbsp;&nbsp; that SK Hynix, Micron, and Samsung make. Then it sends it to an ODM in Taiwan&nbsp;&nbsp;

where they assemble the racks. Nvidia is fundamentally making software that&nbsp;&nbsp; other people are manufacturing, and if software&nbsp; gets commoditized, does Nvidia get commoditized?&nbsp; In the end, something has to&nbsp;

transform electrons to tokens.&nbsp; The transformation of electrons to tokens&nbsp;&nbsp; and making those tokens more valuable over&nbsp; time is hard to completely commoditize.&nbsp; The transformation from electrons to&nbsp;

tokens is such an incredible journey.&nbsp; Making that token is like making one molecule&nbsp; more valuable than another molecule, making&nbsp;&nbsp; one token more valuable than another. The amount of artistry, engineering,&nbsp;&nbsp;

science, and invention that goes&nbsp; into making that token valuable,&nbsp;&nbsp; obviously we're watching it happen in real time. The transformation, the manufacturing, all of the&nbsp;&nbsp; science that goes in there is far from deeply&nbsp;

understood and the journey is far from over.&nbsp; I doubt that it will happen. We're going to make it more efficient, of course.&nbsp; The way that you framed the question&nbsp; is my mental model of our company.&nbsp;

The input is electrons, the output is&nbsp; tokens. In the middle is Nvidia. Our job&nbsp;&nbsp; is to do as much as necessary and as little&nbsp; as possible to enable that transformation&nbsp;&nbsp; to be done at incredible capabilities.

What I mean by "as little as possible,"&nbsp;&nbsp; whatever I don't need to do, I partner with&nbsp; somebody and make it part of my ecosystem.&nbsp; If you look at Nvidia today, we probably&nbsp; have the largest ecosystem of partners,&nbsp;&nbsp;

both in the supply chain upstream and&nbsp; downstream, all of the computer companies,&nbsp;&nbsp; application developers, and model makers. AI is a five-layer cake, if you will.&nbsp; We have ecosystems across the entire five layers.

We try to do as little as possible,&nbsp;&nbsp; but the part that we have to do,&nbsp; as it turns out, is insanely hard.&nbsp; I don't think that gets commoditized. In fact, I also don't think the enterprise&nbsp;&nbsp;

software companies, the tools makers… Most&nbsp; software companies today are tool makers.&nbsp;&nbsp; Some of them are not. Some of them&nbsp; are workflow codification systems.&nbsp; But for a lot of companies, they're tool makers.

For example, Excel is a tool, PowerPoint is a&nbsp;&nbsp; tool, Cadence makes tools, Synopsys makes tools. I actually see the opposite of what people see.&nbsp; I think the number of agents is going&nbsp; to grow exponentially, and the number&nbsp;&nbsp;

of tool users is going to grow exponentially. It's very likely that the number of instances&nbsp;&nbsp; of all these tools is going to skyrocket. It’s very likely that the number of instances&nbsp;&nbsp; of Synopsys Design Compiler is going to&nbsp;

skyrocket, along with the number of agents&nbsp;&nbsp; using the floor planners, our layout&nbsp; tools, and our design rule checkers.&nbsp; Today we're limited by the number of engineers. Tomorrow, those engineers are going to be&nbsp;&nbsp;

supported by a bunch of agents. We're going to be exploring the&nbsp;&nbsp; design space like you've never seen before, and&nbsp; we're going to use the tools that we use today.&nbsp; I think tool use is going to cause&nbsp;

the software companies to skyrocket.&nbsp; The reason why it hasn't happened&nbsp; yet is because the agents aren't&nbsp;&nbsp; good enough at using their tools yet. Either these companies are going to build&nbsp;&nbsp;

the agents themselves, or agents are going to&nbsp; get good enough to be able to use those tools.&nbsp; I think it's going to be a combination of both. I think in your latest filings, you had almost&nbsp;&nbsp; a $100 billion in purchase commitments&nbsp;

with foundries, memory, and packaging.&nbsp; SemiAnalysis has reported that you will have $250&nbsp; billion of these kinds of purchase commitments.&nbsp; One interpretation is that Nvidia's&nbsp; moat is really that you've locked up&nbsp;&nbsp;

One question somebody I was talking to&nbsp; had is, why doesn't Nvidia run multiple&nbsp;&nbsp; different chip projects at the same time&nbsp; with totally different architecture?&nbsp; So you could do something like&nbsp;

a Cerebras-style wafer scale.&nbsp; You could do a Dojo-style huge package. You could do one without CUDA.&nbsp; You have the resources and the engineering&nbsp; talent to do all of these in parallel.&nbsp;

So why put all the eggs in one basket,&nbsp; given who knows where AI might go and&nbsp;&nbsp; architectures might go? Oh, we could. It's just&nbsp;&nbsp; that we don't have a better idea.

We could do all of those things.&nbsp;&nbsp; It's just not better. We simulate it all&nbsp; in our simulator, proveably worse. So we&nbsp;&nbsp; wouldn't do it. We're working on exactly&nbsp; the projects that we want to work on.&nbsp;

If the workload were to change dramatically—and&nbsp; I don't mean the algorithms, I actually mean the&nbsp;&nbsp; workload, and that depends on the shape of the&nbsp; market—we may decide to add other accelerators.&nbsp; For example, recently we added Groq, and we're&nbsp;

going to fold Groq into our CUDA ecosystem.&nbsp; We're doing that now because the value&nbsp; of tokens has gone up so high that&nbsp;&nbsp; you could have different pricing of tokens. Back in the old days, just a couple years ago,&nbsp;&nbsp;

tokens were either free or barely expensive. But now you can have different customers,&nbsp;&nbsp; and those customers want different answers. Because the customers make so much money—for&nbsp;&nbsp; example, our software engineers—if I can&nbsp;

give them much more responsive tokens so&nbsp;&nbsp; that they're even more productive than&nbsp; they are today, I would pay for it.&nbsp; But that market has only recently emerged. So I think we now have the ability to have&nbsp;&nbsp;

the same model, based on the response&nbsp; time, have different segments.&nbsp; That's the reason why we decided to expand&nbsp; the Pareto frontier and create a segment&nbsp;&nbsp; of inference that is faster response&nbsp;

time, even though it's lower throughput.&nbsp; Until now, higher throughput is always better. We think there could be a world where there&nbsp;&nbsp; could be very high ASP tokens, and even&nbsp; though the throughput is lower in the&nbsp;&nbsp;

factory, the ASPs make up for it. That's the reason why we did it.&nbsp; But otherwise, from an architecture perspective,&nbsp; if I had more money, I would put more behind&nbsp;&nbsp; Nvidia’s architecture.

I think this idea of extremely&nbsp;&nbsp; premium tokens and just the disaggregation of&nbsp; the inference market is a very interesting.&nbsp; The segmentation of it. Yeah. Alright, final question. Suppose the deep&nbsp;&nbsp;

learning revolution didn't happen. What would&nbsp; Nvidia be doing? Obviously games, but given—&nbsp; Accelerated computing, the same&nbsp; thing we've been doing all along.&nbsp; The premise of our company is that Moore's&nbsp;

law is going to… General purpose computing&nbsp;&nbsp; is good for a lot of things, but for&nbsp; a lot of computation it's not ideal.&nbsp; So we combined an architecture called&nbsp; a GPU, CUDA, to a CPU, so that we can&nbsp;&nbsp;

accelerate the workload of the CPU. Different kernels of code or&nbsp;&nbsp; algorithms could be offloaded onto our GPU. As a result, you speed up an application by 100x,&nbsp;&nbsp; 200x. Where can you use that? Obviously&nbsp;

engineering and science and physics,&nbsp;&nbsp; data processing, computer graphics,&nbsp; image generation, all kinds of things.&nbsp; Even if AI doesn't exist today,&nbsp; Nvidia would be very, very large.&nbsp;

The reason for that is fairly fundamental, which&nbsp; is that the ability for general purpose computing&nbsp;&nbsp; to continue to scale has largely run its course. And the only way… Not the only way, but the way to&nbsp;&nbsp; do that is through domain-specific acceleration.

One of the domains that we started with was&nbsp;&nbsp; computer graphics, but there are many&nbsp; other domains. There's all kinds.&nbsp;&nbsp; Particle physics and fluids, structured&nbsp; data processing, all kinds of different&nbsp;&nbsp;

types of algorithms that benefit from CUDA. Our mission was really to bring accelerated&nbsp;&nbsp; computing to the world and advance the type of&nbsp; applications that general purpose computing can't&nbsp;&nbsp; do, and scale to the level of capability that&nbsp;

helps break through certain fields of science.&nbsp; Some of the early applications were molecular&nbsp; dynamics, seismic processing for energy discovery,&nbsp;&nbsp; image processing of course, all of those kinds&nbsp; of fields where general purpose computing&nbsp;&nbsp;

is just simply too inefficient to do so. If there were no AI, I would be very sad.&nbsp; But because of the advances that we made in&nbsp; computing, we democratized deep learning.&nbsp; We made it possible for any researcher,&nbsp;

any scientist, anywhere, any student,&nbsp;&nbsp; to be able to access a PC or a GeForce&nbsp; add-in card and do amazing science.&nbsp; That fundamental promise hasn't&nbsp; changed, not even a little bit.&nbsp;

If you watch GTC, there's the whole beginning part&nbsp; of it. None of it's AI. That whole part of it with&nbsp;&nbsp; computational lithography or our quantum chemistry&nbsp; work, data processing work, all of that stuff is&nbsp;&nbsp; unrelated to AI. And it's still very important.&nbsp;

I know that AI is very interesting and quite&nbsp;&nbsp; exciting, but there's a lot of people doing a&nbsp; lot of very important work that's not AI related,&nbsp;&nbsp; and tensors are not the only way that you&nbsp; compute it. We want to help everybody.&nbsp;

Jensen, thank you so much. You're welcome. I enjoyed it.&nbsp; Me too.

> Yall acting like Dwarkesh Destroyed Jensen, but I think his point at 1:20 is a strong compelling argument, but also big ups to this interviewer pushing Jensen hard enough that such a strong multifaceted discussion can come out for us to analyse. Both sides have valid points. 
> 
> Jensen Believes Getting Money, Market share and usage from China keeps USA Ahead by getting more in USA's Tech Stack and moat, as China will be strong regardless thanks to the advantage of their developers, and taking away reasons for using USA Hardware prevents this reliance and drain of resources to the USA, which couldve helped the USA Tech stack strengthen. 
> 
> Dwarkesh is arguing that since there is precedent for China and other tech companies ability to switch to other processors, and that China is Stronger with AI, not giving them NVIDIA helps preserve Americas lead.
> 
> Jensen disagrees that switching processors is Easy, and also feels that Preserving lead in tech is possible, since the leverage of computer science far outweighs the leverage of Compute's Scale, and China wins on that, which is valid. 
> 
> He believes having the High Leverage of Development built on USA's Stack, enhancing and Enriching as well as building reliance on it is what keeps USA Ahead. I think this is a valid argument. While switching Systems is possible, the major dominant player once things reach a level of a new status quo will probably still have the most reliance from others, and its likely their moat will keep growing, as much as people are trying to erode it.
> 
> TLDR: Jensen Believes Selling Chips Builds Reliance on USA, which allows the resources to be funneled into more advances that builds more reliance, and moves the highest leverage actors in the stack, the Devs, onto USA's Hardware, as he believes the reliance, the moat will continue and grow, and make it harder to swap to other processors. As expected, Jensen is bullish on NVIDIA's Moat and prospects.
> 
> Dwarkesh believes no chip = slower ai, and that China Can switch even if they were reliant on NVIDIA to get there in the first place. 
> 
> Fascinating argument that I cant draw the answer as I am no expert, but plenty of unique and enriching perspectives and theories that help expand my mind shared here

> Spicy Jensen is revealing: it's clear what he wants (unfettered access to a largely untapped market) and that safety a very distant secondary/tertiary/etc. concern. Even if he is right, that the sum of all fears could be accomplished today, already, by any motivated 'bad actor', it would still be nice to hear some at-least lip service that a) China's mode of production, and its attendant cultural/societal implications, is inherently adversarial to that of the United States' and b) that 'accelerated computing' has advanced to the point where it has real-world geopolitical implications. He doesn't really acknowledge any of this (other than repeating that the U.S. should be/remain 'ahead') which should be troubling both to audience segments steeped in this debate as well as those coming to it fresh. The question that (perhaps) went unasked is: why aren't you worried about liability? Maybe he feels that hardware is abstracted enough from any specific use case that it's free of accountability for any widespread negative consequences (which would put him in good company with corps. like Raytheon and Boeing). I suppose we'll see if his tune changes once recursive self-improvement becomes widespread among not only frontier but also open-weight models.

> Jensen's argument has historical basis. The GAO found in 2002 that restricting semiconductor equipment exports to China was ineffective because Japanese and European firms kept selling, only ~2 generations behind state-of-the-art. Same story with satellites post-ITAR (Europe built an "ITAR-free" industry that now outcompetes us on price), machine tools (US makers wiped out, we now import from China), and drones (Turkey's Bayraktar, DJI's dominance). There's a historical pattern of unilateral controls accelerating indigenization in the target country while handing market share to allied competitors who aren't restricted. The revenue loss then starves US firms of the R&D budget that created the lead in the first place. You can debate whether AI chips are different because of military dual-use urgency, but dismissing Jensen as self-interested ignores a 40-year pattern.

> Throughout the discussion regarding export controls and the competitive landscape for AI chips, Jensen Huang uses several strong, descriptive terms to push back against certain arguments or characterize specific viewpoints he disagrees with. 
> 
> Childish (1:21:56): Used to describe arguments that operate on extreme, "zero or infinity" premises regarding the impact of providing compute to China.
> Lunacy (1:17:36): Used to characterize the comparison of AI technology to "enriched uranium" and the implications of selling chips for export.
> Torturous (7:15): Used to describe the dense, educational nature of his keynotes where he feels compelled to explain complex supply chain dynamics.
> Lousy (1:17:50, 1:17:51): Used twice to dismiss the "enriched uranium" analogy as an illogical and ineffective way to frame the AI chip situation.
> Narrow-minded (1:25:40): Used to critique policies he believes are overly focused on immediate restrictions without considering the long-term unintended consequences for American industry leadership.
> Horrible (1:33:32): Used to describe the potential outcome of creating two disconnected, global ecosystems where one is built entirely on a foreign tech stack.

Existing models, even quite small ones, with a small amount of fine tuning and a decent harness (neither of which demand heavy compute) could definitely launch effective attacks on the vast majority of important systems out there. The cybersecurity fence just isn't that high and security professionals have been warning about it for years. I'm absolutely certain that offensive Qwens and Gemmas are already out there and if they're not, it wouldn't be hard to make them. Mythos is probably the SotA but you mostly don't need SotA if you want a "cyberweapon" at this point

> Wow!  The temperature got hot in this interview.  Why?  Because Dwarkesh kept hammering at a real hot button for Jensen: the concession of the entire Chinese (and ultimately world) market to China due to concerns over safety.  My analysis: Jensen is correct that: a) open source is the future, b) AI success depends the whole stack (“5 layer cake”), c) export restrictions will result in the (open source) world using China’s stack, d) the US risks losing AI control to China as a result, and e) this would be a terrible outcome for the USA.
> However, Jensen’s fear of a - e (not to mention the economic hit that conceding the China market will cause to Nvidia)  has made him reluctant to acknowledge the real dangers that next-gen AI systems, like Mythos, pose.  An engineer should know you can’t solve a problem unless you acknowledge it first.  Safety concerns are real and getting bigger.  The answer is not to deny that they exist, or minimize them, but rather to get ahead of them – just as Nvidia does with every other engineering problem.  AI safety – properly done -- is a design and engineering problem.  No one does engineering better than Nvidia.  It’s time to step up.  I say this as someone who is a huge fan and stockholder of NVDA.

> 
> Dwarkesh did not have the background knowledge in order to carry out the conversation at his guest's level. Dwarkesh should have been briefed before the interview that open source inference libraries like xLLM has come to the scene, which is a open source Chinese-made inference engine that aims to compete with vLLM but targeted to Huawei's hardware. Dwarkesh also should have introduced his audience to the fact that the latest version of GLM 5.1 and DeepSeek v4 are no longer open source and are running closed source optimized on Chinese hardware. It's probably Jensen's fault not having his company's public relations set up this interview with the background context as a requirement to the publication of this episode.
> 
> I felt like Dwarkesh exposed his age and generational gap between himself and Jensen. Jensen came in with a particular America-first view that he assumed would represent the U.S., but I think Dwarkesh still lacks a nationalistic identity to his show representing the U.S. the way Jensen assumed Dwarkesh would have a certain maturity in his political standing. 
> 
> When Dwarkesh could not keep up with the conversation, he should have paused the interview, gotten the necessary context, then continued once both of them have recovered after being on the same page. Instead this interview seemed like it was released in haste, and if he respected Jensen, would have edited it differently and kept the conversation going until they were on the same page, when I felt like they never quite got there due to Dwarkesh projecting his own experiences into Jensen's point without ever harnessing the awareness that he was doing so.

> ​ @RIURIU4  You're missing the point. The point is that even if chip export controls are a bad idea and it's net good and worthwhile to allow Nvidia to sell chips to China (as there is good reason to believe may be true, e.g. see the Dean Ball x Daniel Kokotajlo Anti-Debate in which the two agree on this point), the uranium analogy still holds. This is because all that is needed for the uranium analogy to be valid is for AI to be a dual-use technology, which it clearly is. You can easily hold the view that "Yes, AI chips are analogous to uranium, because they can both be used for both good and bad purposes, but China isn't so bad, such that the costs associated with China having marginally more powerful dual-use chips are relatively small compared to the benefits of allowing the chip sales to China." In other words, there are a number of ways Jensen could have objected to Dwarkesh's argument against selling chips to China without rejecting the obviously valid analogy that AI chips are like uranium in that they are both dual-use. That's why Jensen's rejection of the analogy was crazy: it makes him look unreasonable and biased in general and there was absolutely no need for him to risk that since there were much better arguments he could have made to defend his position instead.

> There is nothing stopping chinese firms from buying American tokens. I believe that is what he means by "every layer of the stack is important." The 5 layers to which he is referring are these: 
> 
> "Energy — AI needs massive power to run data centers and training workloads.
> 
> Chips — GPUs and other accelerators provide the compute.
> 
> Cloud infrastructure — Networking, orchestration, and data-center systems connect and manage the compute.
> 
> Models — The foundation models that learn from data and generate outputs.
> 
> Applications — The products that turn AI into real economic value, like copilots, robotics, and drug discovery tools."
> 
> 
> 
> He is arguing that in trying to win the model race, we are giving up the infrastructure and chip race, which are arguably more important. And if you lose the chip and cloud then you probably also will lose the application layer. 
> 
>  If you believe that tokens are a comparatively fungible resource (which I personally do), then that would make it the least important layer out of the 5 in the long-run. He argues that if you force China to create their own vertical integration, that it will strengthen them in the long run. Something they would not do unless they were forced to do so. 
> 
> 
> 
> He also alludes to a similar protectionist measure that was taken during Trump 1, which stifled US telecom growth in 2019. Here is Claude's explanation of the telecom example: 
> "The Huawei ban is perhaps the sharpest illustration of Huang's "unintended consequences" argument. In 2019, the US placed Huawei on its Entity List, barring American companies from supplying it with goods, technology, or intellectual property — the security rationale being that China's 2017 Intelligence Law compels Chinese companies to cooperate with state intelligence services on demand, making Huawei-built infrastructure a potential backdoor into critical networks. The problem was that by 2019, the US had no meaningful domestic telecom equipment industry left. Lucent had collapsed and been absorbed by French Alcatel. Nortel had gone bankrupt. Motorola had sold its network division. So when the ban took effect, it didn't redirect contracts to American companies — it redirected them to Ericsson and Nokia, a Swedish and a Finnish firm. The policy successfully neutralized Huawei as a security threat inside the US, which was its stated goal, but it did nothing to establish American control over telecom infrastructure. The US ended up dependent on allied-but-foreign vendors, having neither a Chinese competitor nor an American one. A policy framed around national security arguably left the nation's infrastructure no more sovereign than before.
> 
> "

> There is nothing stopping chinese firms from buying American tokens. I believe that is what he means by "every layer of the stack is important." The 5 layers to which he is referring are these: 
> 
> "Energy — AI needs massive power to run data centers and training workloads.
> 
> Chips — GPUs and other accelerators provide the compute.
> 
> Cloud infrastructure — Networking, orchestration, and data-center systems connect and manage the compute.
> 
> Models — The foundation models that learn from data and generate outputs.
> 
> Applications — The products that turn AI into real economic value, like copilots, robotics, and drug discovery tools."
> 
> 
> 
> He is arguing that in trying to win the model race, we are giving up the infrastructure and chip race, which are arguably more important. And if you lose the chip and cloud then you probably also will lose the application layer. 
> 
>  If you believe that tokens are a comparatively fungible resource (which I personally do), then that would make it the least important layer out of the 5 in the long-run. He argues that if you force China to create their own vertical integration, that it will strengthen them in the long run. Something they would not do unless they were forced to do so. 
> 
> 
> 
> He also alludes to a similar protectionist measure that was taken during Trump 1, which stifled US telecom growth in 2019. Here is Claude's explanation of the telecom example: 
> "The Huawei ban is perhaps the sharpest illustration of Huang's "unintended consequences" argument. In 2019, the US placed Huawei on its Entity List, barring American companies from supplying it with goods, technology, or intellectual property — the security rationale being that China's 2017 Intelligence Law compels Chinese companies to cooperate with state intelligence services on demand, making Huawei-built infrastructure a potential backdoor into critical networks. The problem was that by 2019, the US had no meaningful domestic telecom equipment industry left. Lucent had collapsed and been absorbed by French Alcatel. Nortel had gone bankrupt. Motorola had sold its network division. So when the ban took effect, it didn't redirect contracts to American companies — it redirected them to Ericsson and Nokia, a Swedish and a Finnish firm. The policy successfully neutralized Huawei as a security threat inside the US, which was its stated goal, but it did nothing to establish American control over telecom infrastructure. The US ended up dependent on allied-but-foreign vendors, having neither a Chinese competitor nor an American one. A policy framed around national security arguably left the nation's infrastructure no more sovereign than before.
> 
> "
